text:
The stone circle's energy still thrummed in my ribs as I stepped into the corridor, the pendant at my throat a cold weight. The tarot deck in my hand felt heavier than its gold-leafed edges should have allowed. I didn't look back. The path to the market was one I knew too well—the narrow way that wound through the spice merchants' quarter, where the air always carried the sharp bite of pepper and the slower musk of aged parchment.

The stall came into view: a riot of color under the afternoon sun, bolts of dyed silk hanging like captured rainbows, jars of pigment catching the light, the air thick with the scent of crushed herbs and something sweet and resinous. My contact stood behind the counter, fingers idly tracing the edge of a ledger, her sharp eyes flicking to me with the kind of recognition that came from years of doing business in places where trust was currency and nothing was certain.

I approached, the deck tucked against my palm, the note inside its folds. My fingers found the edge of the tarot card peeking from between two cards—a sharp corner digging into my thumb. The contact's gaze flickered to the deck, then back to my face. Her name was Carys, though no one in the market called her that. To them, she was just a woman with too-keen eyes and a voice that carried like a blade drawn across stone. She tilted her head slightly, the way people do when they're trying to place a face that shouldn't be familiar.

"You're late," she said, voice low enough that the chatter around us swallowed half the words. "Or early. Depends on which clock you're using."

I didn't answer. Instead, I slid the deck across the counter toward her. Not the whole thing. Just the one card. The one that had slipped free when I'd first gripped it in the council chamber: Petition Fate. She didn't touch it. Didn't even look at it directly. But her fingers stilled on the ledger, the tip of her pen hovering just above the page.

Something in the way she held herself shifted. The market noise didn't change. The scent of crushed herbs still hung in the air. But the space between us felt like it had narrowed, the colors of the stall suddenly too bright, too saturated. I watched her eyes—those sharp, watchful things—and saw the moment she recognized what I was asking for. Not the card itself. But what it meant.

Carys exhaled through her nose, a sound that might have been a laugh if it hadn't carried the weight of something like regret. "You're asking for a lot," she murmured. "More than you realize."

I wanted to tell her that I knew exactly what I was asking for. That I'd spent years learning the cost of wishes and the shape of debts they left behind. But the words stuck in my throat, thick as the resinous air. Instead, I reached into my pocket and pulled out the folded note. The wax seal hadn't been broken. Julian's initials were still pressed into the wax, though he hadn't written the note himself. He'd dictated it to someone else, someone who knew the right words to make a merchant's daughter listen.

Carys took the note without touching me. Her fingers brushed the wax, and for a second, I thought she might refuse. Might tell me to take it back, to burn it, to run. But then she tucked it into her sleeve with a movement so precise it looked like she'd practiced it a hundred times.

"The usual terms?" she asked, though we both knew the answer. There were no usual terms anymore. Not after what had happened in the council chamber. Not after the way Julian's ring finger had twitched against the parchment like he was grounding himself against something he couldn't name.

I nodded once, sharp and final. The motion sent a pain lancing through my temple, the kind that came from holding your breath too long. Carys saw it. Of course she did. She always saw too much.

She reached under the counter and pulled out a small scroll, the parchment slightly yellowed at the edges, the fibers uneven in a way that suggested it had been handled more than it should have been. She held it out to me, but not directly. An offering, not a gift. The way you'd pass a knife to someone you trusted not to use it on you.

I took it. The scroll was warm in my hands, as if it had been sitting in the sun. The wax seal on it was still damp. Fresh. The council's iron sigil glistened under the stall's awning, catching the light in a way that made my eyes ache.

Carys's gaze flicked to something over my shoulder. Her expression didn't change, but her fingers tightened around the ledger. "You should go," she said, voice dropping another register. "Before someone notices what you're carrying."

I didn't turn around. Didn't need to. I already knew who was standing there. The air around the stall had gone quiet in that way it did when the world decided to hold its breath.

"Lirael."

The voice was smooth, familiar in a way that made my stomach clench. Not Julian. Not Elara. But close enough to make the pendant at my throat burn cold.

I turned slowly. The vendor—a man with hands like gnarled roots and eyes that had seen too many deals go bad—stood there holding a tray of tiny clay cups. His gaze was locked onto the scroll in my hands. Not the council's seal. Not the fresh wax. But the way the parchment had caught the light, making the fibers glow faintly, like it was lit from within.

Something shifted in his grip. The tray tilted. The cups clinked together, a sound like a warning.

Then the tray slipped.

The cups scattered across the ground, some shattering, others rolling under stalls. The vendor cursed, dropping to his knees to gather them up. But the scroll—it didn't fall. It stayed in my hands, untouched. As if the world itself had decided to keep it safe.

Carys's voice was sharp, cutting through the sudden chaos. "What in the Thirteen—"

The vendor's eyes were locked onto the scroll. Not on me. Not on Carys. Just the parchment. His face went slack, the way people's faces do when they see something they weren't meant to see.

Then he whispered, "Is that a wish?"

The words hung in the air between us, heavy as the resinous air. The scroll in my hands felt like a live thing, its edges pulsing, its fibers trembling.

I didn't answer. Couldn't. My mouth was too dry, my heart too loud in my ears.

Carys's hand closed around my wrist, her grip tight enough to bruise. "Lirael," she said, low and urgent. "You need to decide. Now."

I looked down at the scroll. At the council's seal. At the way the parchment seemed to glow under the stall's awning.

Then I looked at Carys. At the fear in her eyes. At the way her fingers dug into my skin.

And I knew what she was asking me to choose between.

Confront my father. Or confide in Julian.

The pendant at my throat didn't burn anymore. It was ice against my skin. But the scroll in my hand felt like a spark in dry tinder, ready to ignite everything.

I swallowed. "Lead the way."

I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed in it. If only it were that easy. I would wish myself a way out. No — a way in. If only…
